storm.summary_layperson: Thunderstorms visible on radar to the west are currently pulling away from the cove, so the immediate risk here is low, though forecasters say another round could fire up later tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No cells are currently closing on the cove, and even if one did, the marine layer is only weak tonight — a 6.7°F air–water gap now that fades below the protective threshold by about 6:18 PM.
storm.detail_html:
Radar out of KOKX shows a cluster of storm cells 33–48 miles west and WNW of the cove, some topping 55 dBZ, but all of them are currently pulling away — closing speeds are negative (roughly –14 to –18 kt) as the broader system tracks north-northwest at about 21.5 kt. Nothing is presently inbound toward Greenwich, which is why the arrival engine has no active cell to track this run.

Instability is modest right now — HRRR has CAPE at only about 300 J/kg over the cove — but the OKX Area Forecast Discussion flags model guidance building toward 1000–1500+ J/kg later tonight alongside 25–35 kt shear, enough to support a marginal severe thunderstorm risk in a later round. Shear is already strong (34.6 kt), which favors organized cells whenever instability returns.

The Sound's usual defense — cool water holding a stable layer of air that can choke incoming convection — is only weak tonight to begin with (water 73.9°F vs. air 80.6°F, a 6.7°F gap), and it fades fast: the air keeps cooling after sunset while the Sound holds its temperature, so that gap crosses below the ~5°F threshold where the effect matters by around 6:18 PM. Since nothing is closing in tonight, this isn't being tested, but it's worth knowing the buffer won't be there for a late-evening cell.

What would change the call: new cell initiation closer to the cove or a track shift from moving-away to closing — the AFD explicitly calls for a second and possibly third round of showers and thunderstorms through Tuesday night. A Minor Coastal Flood Statement is also in effect for the shoreline starting 10 PM tonight, but that's a tidal issue unrelated to the thunderstorm forecast.

wind.tactics_blurb: A weak, immature sea breeze fills the cove out of the SW around 3–5 kt this evening, fading fast and collapsing near 7:28 PM (about 30 minutes before sunset) — expect a near-calm lull before a light SW background breeze re-establishes after dark. Pressure runs fairly even across the cove with SW flow, maybe a touch stronger toward the mouth and east side; start mid-line and don't expect much to play tactically.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a sea-breeze day (Regime A), but a weak one. The land–water temperature gap (deltaT, the difference between inland air and Sound water temperature) is 6.7°F — enough to clear the 5°F bar that gets a sea breeze going, but well short of the 8°F gate the model uses to call it a mature, fully-developed thermal. The upstream gradient (KBOS/KPVD/KGON backdoor sentinels) is a light W–WNW–WSW flow around 7–14 kt aloft — offshore relative to the cove's south-facing opening — so the surface wind you actually feel is almost entirely the thermal circulation, not a gradient assist.

Establishment is patchy: only about 25% of coastal stations are showing the southerly sea-breeze signature, and direction agreement across the western-LIS station cluster is just 0.68–0.70. HRRR's raw forecast direction (198° SSW) is running about 31° behind what stations are actually reading right now (229° SW) — a real divergence, but since deltaT is below the 8°F maturation gate, the model's veer correction isn't applied. We're trusting the current station read (SW, moderate confidence) over the raw model number for the near-term hours.

With SW flow, the cove's geography runs fairly uniform, with a slight edge in pressure near the mouth and the east side (toward Tod's Point) versus tighter shelter along the west shore. Given the weak, patchy establishment, don't expect the clean oscillating shifts of a mature sea breeze — this reads more as a low, semi-steady flow than a puff-and-shift day.

Sunset is 7:58 PM; the sea breeze is projected to collapse around 7:28 PM, about 30 minutes ahead of it, dropping speeds toward near-calm through 7–8 PM. After the thermal dies, HRRR's own forecast picks a light SW–WSW background gradient back up for the 9–10 PM hours (~5 kt) — that's leftover onshore flow, not a resurgent sea breeze, so don't expect it to build.

On the water: 2–5 kt for most of the window is drifter-class, light-air-specialist conditions; the RC may be watching closely for a postponement if it goes fully calm around the 7–8 PM lull. Bigger boats and one-designs with light-air sails have the advantage tonight.

data_caveats: RAP CAPE/shear unavailable this run — HRRR f01 used for instability/shear, with OKX AFD text as an instability fallback.
Minor Coastal Flood Statement in effect for the shoreline from 10 PM tonight to midnight — tidal, unrelated to the thunderstorm forecast.
Sea-breeze establishment is patchy (only ~25% of coastal stations reading southerly, 0.68–0.70 direction agreement) — wind direction in the early window carries moderate, not high, confidence.
